anchor: all of Al-Fatiha is contained in the Basmala, and all of the Basmala is contained in the letter Ba, and he himself is the dot beneath the Ba
found: Layer4 attributes to Imam Ali a saying widely circulated in Shia sources ('I am the dot beneath the Ba') with no verifiable primary hadith-collection locator; a human should confirm or soften the attribution.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam, explained that when a believer recites the Basmala with true understanding and sincerity, Allah forgives their sins and envelops them in His mercy.
found: Layer4 attributes to Imam Jafar al-Sadiq a hadith about forgiveness through reciting the Basmala that could not be found; the closest located statement from him (in Majma al-Bayan) is instead about the Basmala being 'the greatest verse' in the Quran.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: Imam Ali is reported to have said that when a servant sincerely says 'Alhamdulillah,' Allah grants them a blessing greater than all the material world
found: Layer4 attributes to Imam Ali a saying that 'Alhamdulillah' outweighs the whole material world; the closest match found is a Prophetic hadith recorded in Qurtubi's tafsir (via Nawadir al-Usul, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik), not a saying of Imam Ali.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: Imam Ali is narrated to have said that God's mercy precedes His wrath, and that divine compassion is so vast that even the most hardened sinner should never despair of forgiveness.
found: Layer4 attributes 'God's mercy precedes His wrath' to Imam Ali; this is an authentic hadith qudsi from the Prophet (Bukhari 7453, Muslim 2751, via Abu Hurayrah), not a saying located as Imam Ali's.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: saying that whoever does not show mercy to people will not receive mercy from Allah
found: Layer4 attributes 'whoever does not show mercy to people will not receive mercy from Allah' to Imam al-Sadiq; this is a well-attested Prophetic hadith (Bukhari 7376, Muslim 2319, Tirmidhi 1922, narrated by Jarir ibn Abdullah), not a saying located as Imam al-Sadiq's.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: Al-Tabari notes that the shift to direct address reflects the intimacy and immediacy of the relationship between worshipper and God, a theme echoed in both traditions' mystical literature.
found: Layer5 attributes the 'shift to direct address reflects intimacy/immediacy' point to al-Tabari; a closely matching idea was instead found in Ibn Kathir's commentary on 1:5, not in the al-Tabari text retrieved.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: he is the gate to the city of knowledge that the Prophet represented
found: Layer4 phrases the 'gate to the city of knowledge' hadith as something Imam Ali said about himself; the hadith is actually a statement of the Prophet about Ali, and its authenticity is strongly contested among Sunni hadith critics though accepted in Shia tradition.
note: Migrated from the al-Fatiha first pass (2026-09-02).

anchor: Imam Ali famously said that the hypocrite has two faces and two tongues, praising people in their presence while disparaging them in their absence.
claimed: Imam Ali (a saying of his own)
found: Prophetic hadith on dhu al-wajhayn (the two-faced person), e.g. reported in Sahih al-Bukhari; no specific Imam Ali saying with this wording located
note: The two-faces/two-tongues warning about hypocrites is a well-attested Prophetic hadith, not a traceable saying of Imam Ali; same issue recurs verbatim at 2:14.

anchor: He taught that the greatest blindness is not recognizing the Imam of one's time, as such a person dies the death of ignorance regardless of their religious practices.
found: Prophetic hadith 'man mata wa lam ya'rif imama zamanihi mata mitatan jahiliyyah' (whoever dies without knowing the Imam of his time dies a death of ignorance); Imam al-Sadiq is reported only to have been asked about and explained its meaning, not to have originated it
note: Wikishia's entry on Hadith Man Mata attributes the saying itself to the Prophet; Imam al-Sadiq's role recorded there is exegetical (explaining it means dying in misguidance).

anchor: Many Shia commentators understand that among these names were the blessed names of Prophet Muhammad and his purified family, the Ahlul Bayt.
claimed: Tabatabai (al-Mizan) and Tabrisi (Majma al-Bayan) as representative classical Shia exegetes for the Ahlul-Bayt-names reading
found: Majma al-Bayan's actual commentary on 2:31 gives only mundane interpretations (crafts, geography, languages, angels' names) and quotes Imam al-Sadiq identifying the names as mountains, valleys and plants; al-Mizan quotes the same mundane narration plus one minority report (from Ma'ani al-Akhbar) about 'his hujaj/proofs', not explicitly Muhammad-Ali-Fatima-Hasan-Husain by name
note: The Ahlul-Bayt-names reading is a real minority Shia narration found elsewhere but is not what Tabrisi's Majma al-Bayan or Tabatabai's primary analysis present on this verse; presenting it as the general classical Shia reading overstates the source.

anchor: Imam Ali taught that the most wretched person is one who sells their Hereafter for someone else's worldly gain
found: Not located as a saying of Imam Ali in Shia sources; the closest attested form of this saying ("most wretched/foolish is one who sells his Hereafter for another's worldly gain") is attributed to Imam Malik or Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz in Sunni adab literature
note: One web search found no Shia attribution to Imam Ali; the saying circulates under different, non-Imam names.

anchor: Tabrisi notes that when Imam Ali faced difficulties, he would immediately stand for prayer and recite this verse, demonstrating its practical application in the lives of the Ahlul Bayt
found: al-Kafi narration from Imam al-Sadiq (quoted in al-Mizan's riwaya section on 2:45): kana Ali idha ahalahu amr faza'a qama ila al-salat thumma tala hadhihi al-aya - Majma al-Bayan's own text on 2:45 instead reports this practice of turning to prayer in distress about the Prophet, not Imam Ali
note: Point is real but sourced to al-Kafi/al-Mizan's hadith section, not to Tabrisi's analysis in Majma al-Bayan.

anchor: Imam Jafar al-Sadiq taught that the Jewish scholars of Medina knew from their scriptures that Prophet Muhammad would appear, and some even recognized the descriptions matched him perfectly
found: Majma al-Bayan (Tabrisi) on 2:41 quotes this narration (Hayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b al-Ashraf fearing loss of their yearly stipend from the Jews, so distorting Torah verses describing the Prophet) from Abu Ja'far, i.e. Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, not Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
note: Abu Ja'far (without qualifier) is the kunya of the fifth Imam, al-Baqir; al-Sadiq's kunya is Abu Abdillah.

anchor: Imam Jafar al-Sadiq explained that the Ahlul Bayt will intercede for their sincere followers, but this occurs by divine permission and grace, not as an automatic right
found: Majma al-Bayan (Tabrisi) on 2:48 quotes a hadith marfu' to the Prophet (via Shia narrators): 'I intercede on the Day of Judgment and am granted it, and Ali intercedes and is granted it, and my Ahlul Bayt intercede and are granted it' - a Prophetic saying about the Ahlul Bayt's intercession, not a statement by Imam al-Sadiq
note: The point (Ahlul Bayt intercede by permission) is real but the paragraph credits it to al-Sadiq's own explanation rather than to the Prophetic hadith found in Majma al-Bayan.
